label: Philosophy
title: Do You Really Know Yourself? – The Oldest Advice in Philosophy
thumbnail_text: You know yourself less than you think
description: "Know thyself" was carved at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, and Socrates built a whole way of life around it. But how well can we actually see into our own minds? In this calm video essay we look at the Delphic inscription, Socrates' claim that the unexamined life is not worth living, his famous admission of ignorance – and the 1977 experiments by Nisbett and Wilson, which showed how often we explain our own choices with reasons that were never there.

sections.text:
Imagine someone asks you why you chose your job, your partner, or even the shirt you are wearing today. You would probably have an answer ready. It would sound reasonable. It would feel true.

But what if a good part of that answer was invented on the spot, without you noticing?

Around 2,500 years ago, two words were carved at the most famous temple of the ancient world: know thyself. It sounds like the simplest advice there is. Modern psychology suggests it may be one of the hardest.

sections.heading: Words at the Temple Door
sections.text:
In ancient Greece, people travelled from all over the Mediterranean to Delphi, to ask the oracle of Apollo about wars, marriages and journeys. According to the travel writer Pausanias, several short maxims were inscribed at the entrance of the temple. Another one, nothing in excess, is still quoted today. But the most famous of them was gnōthi seauton. Know thyself.

We do not know for certain who first wrote it. Ancient authors attributed it to various early sages. But its meaning at the time was probably modest. Many scholars read it as a reminder of human limits: know that you are a mortal, not a god. Know your place before the powers you are asking for help.

It was only later that the phrase took on the meaning we usually give it today: look inward, and understand who you really are. And the person who did most to give it that meaning was Socrates.

sections.heading: The Unexamined Life

quote.lead: In Plato's dialogue Phaedrus, Socrates is asked whether he believes the old myths about gods and monsters. He answers that he has no time for such questions, and explains why.
quote.text: I can not, as yet, "know myself," as the Delphic inscription orders; and so it seems to me ridiculous, when I do not yet know that, to investigate irrelevant things.
quote.author: Plato, Phaedrus 229e–230a

sections.text:
For Socrates, knowing yourself was not a side project. It was the main task. Everything else could wait.

At his trial in 399 BC, he was accused of corrupting the young and offending the gods. He could perhaps have saved his life by promising to stop his questioning. He refused. In Plato's Apology, he tells the jury that examining himself and others is the greatest good for a human being, and he adds the sentence that has echoed ever since: the unexamined life is not worth living.

But notice what this examination actually looked like. It did not end in a neat list of answers. Socrates is famous above all for admitting what he did not know. He said that his only advantage over others was that he did not think he knew things he did not know.

Self-knowledge, for Socrates, began with knowing the limits of your knowledge. Including the knowledge you have about yourself.

sections.heading: Telling More Than We Can Know
sections.text:
More than two thousand years later, two psychologists put that insight to the test.

In 1977, Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson published a paper with a memorable title: Telling More Than We Can Know. They had gathered evidence from many studies, including some of their own, which suggested that people often have little direct access to the real causes of their own behaviour.

One of their examples has become well known. In a shop, people were asked to judge which of four pairs of nylon stockings was of the best quality. In fact, the stockings were identical. Yet people strongly favoured the pair on the right-hand side. According to Nisbett and Wilson, the rightmost pair was chosen almost four times as often as the leftmost.

When asked why they chose it, people pointed to the quality, the knit, the elasticity. Nobody mentioned the position. And when the researchers asked directly whether the position might have played a role, almost everyone denied it.

The point is not that these people were lying. They sincerely believed their reasons. They simply could not see the actual cause, so their minds supplied a plausible one.

Nisbett and Wilson noticed something else. The explanations people gave for their own choices were often very similar to the explanations outsiders gave when simply asked to guess. In other words, people seemed to be drawing less on private insight than on general ideas about why someone might act that way.

sections.heading: The Mind as Its Own Storyteller
sections.text:
Later research went even further. In 2005, Petter Johansson, Lars Hall and their colleagues ran an experiment on what they called choice blindness.

Participants were shown two photographs of faces and asked which one they found more attractive. Then, in some trials, the researchers used a sleight of hand to give them the photo they had not chosen, and asked them to explain their choice.

Most of the time, people did not notice the switch. And many of them went on to explain, in detail, why they preferred a face they had actually rejected a moment earlier.

None of this means introspection is worthless. We often know what we feel, and what we want. But when it comes to why, the inner voice that explains us is not always a witness. Sometimes it is more like a storyteller, building a sensible account after the fact.

This is a humbling thought. The reasons we give for our lives are not always the reasons that shaped them. And the more fluent the story, the less we tend to question it.

Socrates might not have been surprised. He never trusted an answer just because it felt certain.

sections.heading: How to Know Yourself Anyway
sections.text:
So if looking inward is unreliable, how can we follow the old advice at all? A few quiet suggestions.

First, watch what you do, not only what you think. Your actions over weeks and months are often a more honest record than your reasons in any single moment. Where does your time actually go? What do you return to without being asked?

Second, ask others. People who know you well can sometimes see patterns you cannot, simply because they are not inside them. Listening without arguing is a skill in itself. You do not have to accept every judgment. But a pattern that several people notice independently is worth taking seriously.

Third, hold your explanations lightly. When you catch yourself saying, I did it because, add a quiet question: is that really why? Or is that the story that sounds best?

And finally, keep asking. For Socrates, self-knowledge was never a finished possession. It was a practice, done every day, in conversation.

sections.heading: A Lifelong Conversation
sections.text:
The words at Delphi do not promise that you will ever fully know yourself. Perhaps no one does. The mind is too deep, and too good at telling stories.

Every few years, we look back and realise we misread something about ourselves: a fear we called caution, a habit we called a choice.

But that is not a reason to stop looking. It is a reason to look with more humility, and more curiosity.

Know thyself may not be an answer you reach. It may be a conversation you keep having, for the rest of your life, with the stranger you are closest to.

short.title: Do you really know why you do things?
short.hook: Why did you really choose that?
short.text:
In 1977, two psychologists described a simple test. People were asked to pick the best of four pairs of nylon stockings. The stockings were identical. Yet people strongly favoured the pair on the right.

When asked why, they talked about quality and texture. Nobody mentioned the position. Asked directly, almost everyone denied it.

They were not lying. They simply could not see the real cause, so their minds supplied a plausible one.

Two and a half thousand years ago, the temple at Delphi gave one piece of advice: know thyself. It may be harder than it sounds.
